To us, love is everything. But what is love to you?
Share with us your own perspective:

venue.title: The Place
venue.body:
Keralam may seem a far-away land to you. It sits calmly on the small southwest coast of India, a bit far from the chaos of invasions and wars historically. Because of this, people of this region have had enough time to develop a culture that puts harmony and coexistence as its foundation. This small piece of land, with its humble people and lush green forests and fresh waters and mighty coastlines, will make you feel at home easily once you open yourself to embrace the differences. You are entering one of the oldest lands on earth, where people of different faiths and cultures have happily lived in brotherhood since 50 CE. Hence, we can be sure that people here will never make you feel left out.  Here you can easily see a church, temple, mosque, and synagogue coexisting a few meters away from each other. Hence, we celebrate festivals of all faiths together. 

So welcome to Keralam, ' God's Own Country'.


Any part of Kerala is very beautiful in its own way. But we would like to welcome you to this specific part of Kerala because it is very close to our heart. There is a very specific historical gate in this region of Thrissur. This is an important region that was actively communicating with the distant world through maritime trade relations. The Jews were among the first foreign settlers in the region. It is believed that the Apostle  St.Thomas arrived here in 50 CE. In 52 CE, the first church is built by St.Thomas, which is located in Palayur, Thrissur. Kerala was also one of the major port cities in Roman times; the port of Muziris is not too far from here. The Arab merchants were the connectors who sailed from the ports of Keralam to Europe with luxury goods (silk, artisanal crafts), arms, and spices. They were also some of the early settlers in Kerala. They built Cheraman Juma Masjid in 629 CE in Kodungalloor (Muzris), Thrissur. This region is also dear to us as it has been the cradle of poetry, art, and dance forms . Also, this region is home to Sangamagrama Madhava,  who founded the Kerala School of Astronomy and Mathematics  in 14th century that produced some of the greatest Indian mathematicians and astronomers.  Too many special coincidences of history landed right here that inspired our lives and our everyday conversations. As this region welcomed a lot of guests from distant lands throughout history, who later got assimilated with us so seamlessly, we would also like to host you for our wedding exactly here.

We have arranged your stay at a heritage resort on the banks of the Nila River, also called Bharathapuzha. Once the summer palace of the Maharajas of Cochin, it now hosts a serene Ayurvedic resort, The River Retreat, a heritage Ayurvedic Resort in the Thrissur district. These riverbanks have been a historical witness and have shaped the culture of Kerala. This region has hosted a lot of ancient festivals, symposium on art, literature and history. Hence, you could explore a few art museums and the Academy of Culture (Kerala Kalamandalam) here.

care.title: Reception
care.body:
Dear guests,

Before, during and after the wedding, we would like you to feel at home in Kerala, as we do. The people of Kerala warmly welcomed their guests throughout the whole history, recognising in them God (Adithi Devo Bhava) and treating them alike; indeed, we simply follow their example.

Nevertheless, we know that, for many of you, this will be the first time travelling to India. India is indeed a huge and far away country, so that such a trip to an exotic and unexplored place may seem, at first, overwhelming. For this reason we set up this page, where to provide you some basic information about your future trip to Kerala and, most importantly, to collect information about your travelling plan, so that we can conveniently take care of you at your arrival and during the three wedding days. Moreover, this page allows you to communicate to us all your special needs for the travel and stay, so that we can organize accordingly.

Yours sincerely,

Sariga and Stefano

cabinet.title: Treasure
cabinet.body:
Dearest Guests,

You are our treasure! Your presence in our celebration is our greatest gift. So please kindly do not gift us anything. Let us enjoy a week together singing and dancing, and take this as an opportunity to have a big get-together for all of us. Looking forward to sharing with you our small joy.


With Love,
Sariga and Stefano

rituals.title: The Rituals
rituals.kicker: In the beginning,  Love arose,  which was the primal germ cell of the mind. The Seers, searching in their hearts with wisdom, discovered the connection of Being in Nonbeing. Who really knows? Who can presume to tell it? Whence was it born? Whence issued this creation? Even the Gods came after its emergence. Then who can tell from whence it came to be?           -Rig Veda(10.129.4),Nasadiya Sukta (Hym of creation)

events.description: The wedding celebrations begin with honouring the elders. With their blessings, the bride and groom are taken for the royal bath, where family and friends apply a ceremonial cream made of sandalwood, saffron and milk. This is followed by a traditional bath with water infused with fragrant flowers and herbs, symbolising purification and the rejuvenation of the youthful body and mind before the sacred wedding ceremonies.

events.title: Prasādana
events.subtitle: Adornment
events.description: The bride and groom are now adorned and celebrated by their families and friends. Mehndi (henna) is used to decorate the bride’s hands, while the Tilak ceremony is performed for the groom. The bride’s brother applies a sandalwood mark to the groom’s forehead, welcoming him as a new member of the family. In accepting the Tilak, the groom in turn expresses his promise to embrace his new role with love and great care.

destinations.name: Cheruthuruthy & the Nila
destinations.history: Cheruthuruthy rests beside the Bharathapuzha — affectionately called the Nila — a river deeply embedded in Kerala’s literary, artistic and cultural memory. The village is also home to Kerala Kalamandalam, one of the institutions most closely associated with the teaching and preservation of Kerala’s classical performing traditions.
destinations.thingsIntro: This is the easiest place to experience slowly during the wedding days: river light, village roads, performance traditions and the quiet landscape around the Nila.

destinations.name: Thrissur
destinations.history: Thrissur is often called Kerala’s cultural capital. Its historic centre grew around the Vadakkunnathan Temple and the great circular Swaraj Round; the city remains closely associated with festivals, music, theatre, museums and Kerala’s modern cultural institutions.
destinations.thingsIntro: A comfortable half-day or day trip for guests who want an introduction to Kerala’s temple-town urbanism, museums, local food and shopping.

destinations.name: Malampuzha
destinations.history: Malampuzha lies at the foot of the Western Ghats near Palakkad. The reservoir and garden landscape became one of the region’s best-known leisure areas, framed by the mountains that define the Palakkad Gap.
destinations.thingsIntro: Best as a relaxed excursion rather than a rushed checklist: combine the reservoir landscape with gardens and the mountain edge.

destinations.name: Kollengode
destinations.history: Kollengode lies in southern Palakkad beneath the Western Ghats, in a landscape of paddy fields, old houses, temples and mountain horizons. It offers a gentler, less touristic impression of inland Kerala.
destinations.thingsIntro: Come for the landscape and old-town atmosphere. It works beautifully together with nearby countryside and foothill drives.

destinations.name: Nelliyampathy
destinations.history: Nelliyampathy is a hill landscape in the Western Ghats above Palakkad, reached through winding forest and plantation roads. Tea, coffee and other plantation landscapes alternate with viewpoints and protected forest.
destinations.thingsIntro: A good choice for guests wanting mountains without travelling as far as Munnar or Wayanad. Allow a full day and avoid over-packing the schedule.

destinations.name: Wayanad
destinations.history: Wayanad is a highland district of forests, plantations, valleys and ancient human settlement. Its landscape connects Kerala with the Deccan plateau and carries archaeological, tribal and colonial layers quite distinct from central Kerala.
destinations.thingsIntro: Do not treat Wayanad as a day trip from the wedding. Two or three nights allow time for forests, viewpoints and archaeological sites without spending the entire visit in a car.

destinations.name: Fort Kochi & Mattancherry
destinations.history: Fort Kochi and Mattancherry preserve centuries of Indian Ocean exchange. Arab, Jewish, Portuguese, Dutch, British and local communities all left traces in the harbour quarter: churches, synagogues, palaces, warehouses, spice streets and waterfront architecture.
destinations.thingsIntro: Walk rather than rush. The pleasure is in moving between the waterfront, old streets, galleries, religious buildings and the spice quarter.

destinations.name: Munnar & Eravikulam
destinations.history: Munnar’s modern landscape was shaped by plantation history in the high Western Ghats. Nearby Eravikulam National Park protects montane grassland and shola habitat and is especially associated with the endangered Nilgiri tahr.
destinations.thingsIntro: Give Munnar time. The most rewarding version is not a sequence of viewpoints but a slower stay with one or two walks, tea-country drives and a visit to Eravikulam when access is open.

destinations.name: Kumarakom & Vembanad
destinations.history: Kumarakom sits on Vembanad, the great lake at the heart of Kerala’s backwater system. Canals, rice landscapes, village settlements and water transport produce a rhythm entirely different from the mountains or coast.
destinations.thingsIntro: The point here is slowness. A lake stay and a smaller canoe or responsible backwater trip are often more memorable than spending the whole day on a large houseboat.

destinations.history: The Muziris region evokes Kerala’s ancient maritime connections with the wider Indian Ocean and Mediterranean worlds. Archaeology and later monuments around Kodungallur and North Paravur reveal successive Jewish, Christian, Islamic and local histories of exchange.
destinations.thingsIntro: This is the Kerala suggestion for guests interested in history rather than scenery alone. The sites are dispersed, so a car and a curated half-day or full day works best.

beyond.sectionNote: If you have a little more time, these are four journeys we would suggest after the wedding — ways of making the return journey itself part of India.

journeys.name: The Konkan & Deccan Journey
journeys.route: Kerala → Badami → Hampi → Goa → Mumbai → Ajanta & Ellora
journeys.bestFor: History · rock-cut architecture · rail scenery · coast
journeys.description: Our grand overland suggestion. Travel north from Kerala into the Early Chalukya country around Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal, continue to the ruined imperial landscape of Hampi, then cross toward Goa and the western coast before travelling onward to Mumbai. Ajanta and Ellora are not an optional afterthought here: they are a major historical climax of the journey and deserve dedicated days.
journeys.travelNotes: The train is part of the experience, not merely transport. On suitable rail segments, choose daylight travel and window-facing seats where possible. Western Ghats scenery can include forests, steep valleys, bridges and the spectacular Dudhsagar Falls landscape; Dudhsagar is a view from the rail journey, not a required stop. Exact train services and routings should be checked for the travel date. Guests short on time can replace selected rail legs with domestic flights, especially between Kochi, Goa and Mumbai.
journeys.departure: A natural finish is Mumbai, with extensive international connections to Europe. Ajanta and Ellora require an inland Maharashtra extension; plan the route deliberately rather than treating them as stops on the Konkan Railway.

landmarks.name: Badami · Aihole · Pattadakal
landmarks.history: Together these sites form one of the most important early-medieval architectural landscapes of the Deccan. Badami’s rock-cut sanctuaries, Aihole’s extraordinary experimentation with temple forms and Pattadakal’s ceremonial monuments show architectural ideas developing across regions and traditions.
landmarks.thingsIntro: Give the group at least a full day, preferably longer. The value lies in seeing the three places as one architectural conversation rather than as isolated monuments.

landmarks.name: Hampi
landmarks.history: Hampi preserves the monumental remains of Vijayanagara, one of South India’s great imperial capitals, within an unforgettable landscape of granite boulders and the Tungabhadra River. Sacred complexes, markets, royal enclosures and water systems spread across a vast archaeological zone.
landmarks.thingsIntro: Two full days is far better than one rushed circuit. Divide the sacred-centre and royal-centre landscapes and leave one sunrise or sunset free simply to experience the terrain.

landmarks.name: Goa
landmarks.history: Goa combines an Indian Ocean coastal landscape with several centuries of Portuguese colonial history and older regional traditions. Old Goa’s churches, Fontainhas, village houses and the coast make it much more than a beach stop.
landmarks.thingsIntro: Stay two nights if possible. Keep one historical half-day for Old Goa and Panjim, then leave space for the sea and slower village landscapes.

landmarks.name: Mumbai
landmarks.history: Mumbai is both a historic port and one of India’s defining modern cities. Gothic and Indo-Saracenic civic architecture, Art Deco, markets, the harbour and dense neighbourhoods reveal very different periods of urban history.
landmarks.thingsIntro: Two nights gives a first impression and also makes Mumbai a practical international departure point.

landmarks.name: Ajanta Caves
landmarks.history: Ajanta’s caves were excavated in a horseshoe-shaped ravine and contain Buddhist monastic and devotional spaces from different periods. The surviving murals are among the great achievements of ancient Indian painting and reward slow looking rather than a hurried photographic visit.
landmarks.thingsIntro: Allow a dedicated day. Arrive early, use the site transport system and give the painted caves time; low light and conservation rules are part of the experience.

landmarks.name: Ellora Caves
landmarks.history: Ellora brings Buddhist, Hindu and Jain rock-cut monuments into a single extraordinary complex. Its centrepiece, the Kailasa Temple, was carved downward from living rock on a monumental scale and is one of the most astonishing architectural works in India.
landmarks.thingsIntro: Give Ellora a full day if you care about architecture. Do not see only Kailasa and leave; the sequence of Buddhist and Jain caves explains the site's breadth.

journeys.name: Lakshadweep · Into the Arabian Sea
journeys.bestFor: Sea · coral lagoons · rest after the wedding
journeys.description: For guests who want the opposite of a monument-filled journey: travel from Kochi into the Lakshadweep archipelago for coral lagoons, clear water and an intentionally slow island stay. Lakshadweep is a Union Territory, not part of Kerala, although Kochi is an important gateway.
journeys.travelNotes: Entry permits are required and transport and accommodation are more limited than on the mainland. Flights and authorised packages should be planned well in advance. Reef-sensitive travel matters: choose responsible operators and follow local environmental restrictions.
journeys.departure: Return through Kochi for onward international travel to Europe. Because schedules can be limited, keep a buffer before a long-haul flight.

landmarks.name: Agatti
landmarks.history: Agatti is one of the principal air gateways to Lakshadweep and is surrounded by a long turquoise lagoon and coral reef system.
landmarks.thingsIntro: Use Agatti as an arrival point and, depending on permits and transport, as a base or transfer point to quieter islands.

landmarks.name: Bangaram & Thinnakara
landmarks.history: The Bangaram–Thinnakara area is known for small-island scale, lagoon water and reef scenery rather than urban attractions.
landmarks.thingsIntro: Come here to do less: swim, snorkel, walk the sand and let the island rhythm replace the mainland itinerary.

journeys.name: Dravidian Land
journeys.route: Palakkad → Chettinad → Keeladi & Madurai → Srirangam → Chola Country → Mahabalipuram → Chennai
journeys.bestFor: Archaeology · temple architecture · food · living cities
journeys.description: A journey eastward from Kerala into Tamil country, moving from mercantile mansions and archaeology to living temple cities, the monumental Chola landscape and finally the Pallava shore at Mahabalipuram. It is best understood as a historical progression rather than a collection of isolated temples.
journeys.travelNotes: Road and rail can be combined depending on pace. A private car is particularly useful through Chettinad and the Chola temple region, while major cities have good rail connections. Temple access, dress and photography rules vary and should always be respected.
journeys.departure: Finish in Chennai, which has extensive domestic and international air connections and makes a logical departure point for Europe.

landmarks.name: Chettinad
landmarks.history: The Chettinad region is associated with the Nattukottai Chettiar mercantile community, whose wealth and international trading networks produced remarkable mansions blending local planning with materials and decorative influences from across Asia and Europe.
landmarks.thingsIntro: Stay in a restored mansion if possible. The architecture, courtyards, tiles, woodwork and food are the experience.

spots.name: Athangudi

spots.name: Chettinad mansion walks

stays.name: The Bangala
stays.note: Celebrated heritage stay and culinary destination.

landmarks.name: Keeladi & Madurai
landmarks.history: Keeladi has become an important archaeological site for understanding early historic settlement in the Vaigai valley. Nearby Madurai adds the continuous life of one of South India’s great temple cities, centred on the Meenakshi–Sundareswarar complex.

stays.name: Heritage Madurai
stays.note: Resort-style property incorporating modernist architectural heritage.

stays.name: Sangam Hotel Trichy

ritualsInfo.leftText:
In a village in Kerala, or a hotel ballroom in Hannover, or a temple courtyard in Rajasthan,  a priest recites verses that begin with the word satyena, “by truth.” The bride circles a fire. The groom takes her hand. Seven steps are walked. These acts do not merely echo the Rigveda (RV); in many cases, the words being chanted are from the Rigveda, drawn from a single hymn composed somewhere in the modern-day Punjab perhaps thirty-five centuries ago.

RV 10.85, known in the tradition as the Suryasukta or the Vivahasukta (the “wedding hymn”), is the most sustained account of social and ritual life anywhere in the Rigvedic corpus. Its forty-seven verses narrate the celestial marriage of Surya (the Sun-maiden, daughter of Savitr ie Sun) to Soma, and in doing so they lay down a template for every human wedding that followed. No other hymn in the collection describes clothing, chariots, bridal attendants, apotropaic charms against evil spirits, the giving of gifts to priests, the bride’s journey to her new home, and the expectation that she will “address the assembly” as a figure of household authority. It is, in the strict sense, a liturgical script: the Grhya Sutras (the later manuals of domestic ritual) take this hymn and build an entire wedding ceremony around it, verse by verse.

What makes this remarkable is not just the hymn’s antiquity. It is the unbroken continuity. The saptapadi (seven steps around the fire), the panigrahana (grasping of the hand), the invocation of Agni as witness: these are not revivals or reconstructions. They are the same ritual acts, performed with the same (or closely related) words, that RV 10.85 prescribes. The hymn is one of the longest-lived liturgical texts in human history. It has outlived the civilisation that composed it, the language in which it was first spoken, and many of the gods to whom it was addressed. What follows is a close reading: what the hymn says, what scholars have argued about it, and what it reveals about how the Vedic poets understood the joining of two lives.

The major steps in the wedding Ceremony is : 

Varapuja (honouring the groom): The bride’s family welcomes the groom, corresponding to the Rigvedic scene of Savitar bestowing Surya.
Kanyadana (gift of the maiden): The father gives away the bride, echoing RV 10.85.9 where Savitar bestows his daughter.
Panigrahana (hand-grasping): The groom takes the bride’s right hand, formalised in the Grhya Sutras from AV 14.1.48.
Agni Parikrama (circumambulation of fire): The couple circles the sacred fire, with Agni as witness, directly drawn from the Rigvedic insistence on Agni as “leader of the train” (RV 10.85.8).
Saptapadi (seven steps): The couple takes seven steps together, each representing a vow. The Paraskara Grhya Sutra (I.8.1-2) prescribes seven steps northward, each with its own invocation.
Laja Homa (offering of parched grain): The bride offers grain into the fire, a rite that echoes the broader Vedic fire ritual tradition.
Ashmarohana (stepping on a stone): The bride places her foot on a stone, symbolising steadfastness

In the vedic hymns, the bride and the groom are embodied as two celestial beings about to merge as the poem is sung in the background. That confirms the sacred wedding.
left.storyText:
Before the poem becomes the story of a human wedding, it begins in the cosmos.

Sūryā, the solar daughter, is preparing to leave her home as the bride. Around her, ordinary objects become cosmic things. Her bridal journey is imagined through images: thought becomes her bridal couch, sight becomes an adornment for her eyes, and mind transforms into her chariot.  Raibhī, Nārāśaṃsī, Gāthā (different types of music, sacred verse, praises, songs) accompany her as bridesmaids. Sky and earth become her bridal chest of treasure. 

Before the bride embraces the groom in his human form, she is married to the Soma (divine elixir of the moon), then the Gandarva (Divine lover), and the Agni ( Fire). 

Poem says
       "Soma first obtained the bride; the Gandharva obtained her next. Agni was your third husband; your fourth husband is born of man"

The twin Aśvins (twin horsemen in the Aries constellation) appear as the groomsmen, while Savitṛ (Sun) sends the daughter forth. Soma represents infancy and nourishment (milk), waxing and waning of the moon is imaged as seasons; Gandharva represents adolescence, passion, and the arts (music, dance); Agni represents the mental maturity and readiness for marriage. The bridal chariot carries her away from the world she knows and towards another household. 

Beneath all this cosmic imagery lies something deeply human: a daughter is leaving home.
The hymn worries about the road before her. It asks that dangers withdraw from her path. It blesses the journey and surrounds the bride with divine protection as she crosses the threshold between one household and another. Eventually the celestial imagery gives way to the human ceremony. Agni, the sacred fire, stands at the threshold between them. The groom takes the bride's hand and asks that they reach old age together. They together take the seven steps of life around the sacred fire, chanting seven wows, while the groom leads the first 4 steps and steps back for the bride to lead the rest, symbolising how life takes its turns and how one has to lead the family when the other feels weaker. 

The poem encloses, by vesting the bride supreme power in her new household, the bride is told to “rule as samrajni (an empress)", over her new life. She is told to be sovereign for herself in the new family with her husband's parents and his siblings. The Vedic wedding hymn confers authority, not merely permission, on the bride within her new household. The closing verses imagine husband and wife remaining together through the full span of life, surrounded by children and grandchildren. 

A marriage imagined across the cosmos has become something profoundly human: a daughter leaves home, a journey begins, a hand is taken, and two people are asked to grow old together
left.bridgeText: The celestial story has now become a human ritual for the last 35 centuries.

cosmic.heading: “Truth is the base that bears the earth; by Surya are the celestial world sustained. By Law the Adityas stand secure, and Soma holds his place in cosmos.”
cosmic.title: Cosmic Architecture
cosmic.body:
The wedding hymn begins not with bride or groom, but with the structure of the universe. Truth, cosmic order, Earth, the Sun and Moon establish the world in which the marriage will unfold.
This opening deliberately places marriage within a larger cosmos.  Before Sūryā begins her journey as a bride, the poet first establishes the universe around her.
Soma dominates these opening verses. The poem plays with the distinction between the Soma known ritually on earth (sacred drink) and a celestial Soma; this section is also important in the history of Soma's developing association with the Moon.

preparation.title: The Bride’s Preparation
preparation.heading: “Thought was the pillow of her couch, sight was the unguent for her eyes; her treasury was earth and sky when Surya went unto her husband"”
preparation.body:
The cosmic prologue ends at verse 5. From verse 6, the hymn shifts register, and we are suddenly in the middle of a wedding. Raibhi is the bride’s dear friend; Narasamsi leads her home. The poet names her attendants, her garments, her cosmetics. 

 Thought became her pillow. The “unguent for her eyes” is at once a literal cosmetic practice (collyrium, anjana, applied to a bride’s eyes) and a cosmic metaphor: sight itself adorns the solar daughter. The sky and earth became her treasures.  The bridal chariot is described in verse 8 with similar doubling: “Hymns were the cross-bars of the pole, Kurira-metre decked the chariot, mind was her wagon, and sky was her canopy, and  Agni (fire) was leader of the carriage. Soma was the bridegroom, the Aśvins were both wooers, when Savitar gave Sūryā to her husband, as she pronounced (her vow) with her (whole)mind. The chariot of the cosmic bride is constructed from liturgical elements: chandas (metre) forms its frame; Vedic hymns are its crossbars.

chariot.title: The Chariot and the stars
chariot.heading: “Surya’s bridal procession, which Savitur despatched, has advanced; the oxen are driven forth in Magha; she is borne to her husband’s house in the Arjuni constellations.”
chariot.body:
The bridal procession is described in astronomical terms. Verse 13 names specific naksatras (lunar mansions): “In Magha days are oxen slain, in Arjunis they wed the bride.” The reference to Magha and Arjuni (Phalguni) places the wedding at a particular point in the lunar calendar, linking the ritual to the Vedic astronomical system that governed the timing of sacrifices and rites of passage.

The chariot itself is described in verse 20 with remarkable specificity:
“Ascend the chariot made of kims’uka wood and s’almali, all-shaped, gold-hued, with strong wheels, light-rolling, bound for the world of life immortal; make for thy lord a happy bridal journey.”

The kimsuka (Butea monosperma, the flame-of-the-forest, known for its brilliant orange-red flowers) and salmali (Bombax ceiba, the silk-cotton tree) are not arbitrary. Both trees were associated with fertility and auspiciousness in Vedic culture. The chariot is “gold-hued” (hiranyavarnam), establishing the solar colour that marks the bride throughout the hymn.

Verses 14 to 16 introduce a puzzling detail: the Asvins arrive on a three-wheeled chariot, but one wheel is hidden. “Where was one chariot wheel of yours?” the poet asks. The Brahmans “who are skilled in highest truths” know its location (10.85.16). This takes this as a reference to the invisible or esoteric dimension of ritual knowledge: what is visible in the ceremony is not all there is.

journey.title: The Bridal Journey & Protections
journey.heading: "Let highwaymen who lie in wait not find the married couple.Let them cross over the hard place by easy roads. Let hostilities run away."
journey.body: The Vedic wedding, for all its cosmic grandeur, was also an occasion of acute anxiety. The bride was leaving her natal family. The journey was literal (by chariot, along roads that might be dangerous) and symbolic (from one ritual sphere to another). The apotropaic verses address both registers. They protect against actual bandits on the road and against invisible malevolences that might attach themselves to the bride’s garments or body.

threeHusbands.title: Three Husbands Before the Human One
threeHusbands.heading: “Soma first obtained the bride; the Gandharva obtained her next. Agni was your third husband; your fourth husband is born of man.”
threeHusbands.body:
The three divine husbands are read as stages of a woman’s maturation. Soma represents infancy and nourishment (milk); Gandharva represents adolescence and the arts (music, dance); Agni represents the domestic fire, cooking, and readiness for marriage. Under this reading, the verse describes not sequential marriages but sequential developmental phases.

 The Gandharva (divine lover) appears also in verses 21 to 22, where he is directly asked to leave the bride: 
“Rise up from hence, Visvavasu: with reverence we worship thee. Seek thou another willing maid, and with her husband leave the bride.” 
It ensures that the divine claimant relinquishes his hold before the human wedding proceeds. This is to symbolise that the bride should not be captivated by impulsive adolescence and make a marriage decision out of teenage passion. The union with Gandharva depicts the intense, passionate mind of the adolescent girl.

authority.title: The Bride’s Authority
authority.heading: “Go to your home, to be the lady of the house; with authority you will address the vidatha. Prosper here, beloved, with your children; in your home, watch over the household.”
authority.body:
Perhaps the most striking passage in the hymn, for a modern reader, is the instruction given to the bride as she arrives at her new home.

The word vidatha is significant. It refers to a public assembly or gathering where important matters were discussed. The bride is not merely told to manage domestic affairs in private; she is told she will “address the assembly” with authority, even in old age. This is a public role, a recognition of social voice.

The closing verses reinforce this:

Verse 42: “Be ye not parted; dwell ye here, reach the full time of human life. With sons and grandsons sport and play, rejoicing in your own abode.”
Verse 45: “O Bounteous Indra, make this bride blest in her sons and fortunate. Vouchsafe to her ten sons, and make her husband the eleventh man.”
Verse 46: “Over thy husband’s father and thy husband’s mother bear full sway. Over the sister of thy husband,  over his brothers rule sovereign.”

handFire.title: The Hand & the Fire
handFire.heading: "I grasp your hand for good fortune, so that with me as your husband you will reach old age."
handFire.body:
Here the celestial imagery gives way to one of the most enduring gestures of the Vedic wedding: the taking of the bride’s hand.
Before Agni, the sacred fire, the groom takes Sūryā’s hand and asks that they may grow old together. The gods are invoked not merely as witnesses, but as those who have brought the bride and groom together and entrusted them to a shared household life.
Agni stands at the threshold between the divine and the human. As the sacrificial fire, he carries offerings towards the gods; within the wedding hymn, he also accompanies the bride on her passage towards human marriage. The hand taken before the fire therefore marks more than a union between two people: it is the moment when the celestial story enters the human home.

The gesture survives in the Vedic marriage rite as Pāṇigrahaṇa — “the taking of the hand.” In RV 10.85.36, the groom says:

“I take your hand for good fortune,
so that with me, your husband,
you may reach old age.”

atharvaveda.title: Atharva Veda: A parallel Wedding Poem
atharvaveda.body:
The Rigvedic wedding hymn does not stand alone. Atharva Veda Book 14 contains two extended hymns (AV 14.1 and 14.2) that closely parallel and expand upon RV 10.85. Many verses are shared verbatim between the two collections, while the Atharva Veda adds material that is more explicitly concerned with the physical details of the ceremony.

AV 14.1.1, for example, opens with the same cosmological declaration as RV 10.85.1: “By truth is the earth established; by the sun is the sky established.” But the Atharva Veda adds extended passages on the hand-grasping ceremony (panigrahana): “Wherewith Agni grasped the right hand of this earth, therewith grasp I thy hand; do not stagger in company with me, with both progeny and riches” (AV 14.1.48). This is a direct ritual instruction, specifying what the groom says as he takes the bride’s hand.

right.title: The Wedding Ceremony
right.intro: The Grhya Sutras (literally “threads of domestic ritual”), composed roughly between the eighth and fourth centuries BCE, take the raw material of RV 10.85 and the Atharva Veda wedding hymns and systematise them into step-by-step procedural manuals. The most important of these for the wedding ceremony are the Ashvalayana Grhya Sutra (associated with the Rigveda), the Paraskara Grhya Sutra (associated with the Shukla Yajurveda), and the Gobhila Grhya Sutra (associated with the Samaveda). The main steps during the wedding day are briefed below.

varapuja.title: Varapūjā
varapuja.subtitle: Honouring the groom
varapuja.body:
The bride’s family and the groom correspond to the Rigvedic scene of Savitar bestowing Surya. 
The feet of the groom are washed by the bride’s father to welcome the groom as Mahavishnu Svarupaya varahaya, i.e., Maha Vishnu (God) himself, and the bride as Lakshmi (Goddess). The father of the bride washes the feet of the groom with milk, saffron, and roses, then with holy water, and wipes with a silk towel. Then the bride’s father and the bridegroom’s father face each other, solemnise the final betrothal ceremony, with the Vedic priest chanting the relevant hymns, in which the Ghotras & names of the bride, the bridegroom, as well as the names of their three generations of ancestors, are recited in the presence of friends, relatives, and invitees.

kanyadana.title: Kanyādāna
kanyadana.subtitle: Gift of the maiden
kanyadana.body: The father gives away the bride, echoing RV 10.85.9, where Savitar (Sun) bestows his daughter.The bride is made to sit on her father’s lap and is given away as gift by him, to the bridegroom.

panigrahana.title: Pāṇigrahaṇa
panigrahana.subtitle: The taking of the hand
panigrahana.body: This means "holding hands". The groom holds the hand of the bride. The Manthras say: The Devas have offered you to me in order that I may live the life of a householder ( GRIHASTA ); we shall not part from each other even after we grow old?

agniParikrama.title: Agni Parikrama
agniParikrama.subtitle: Around the sacred fire
agniParikrama.body: The couple circles the sacred fire, with Agni as witness, directly drawn from the Rigvedic insistence on Agni as “leader of the train” (RV 10.85.8).

saptapadi.title: Saptapadī — The Seven Steps
saptapadi.subtitle: The seven vows
saptapadi.intro: The couple takes seven steps together, each representing a vow. The Paraskara Grhya Sutra (I.8.1-2) prescribes seven steps northward, each with its own invocation. The groom leads the first 4 steps, and then he steps back for the bride to lead the rest. This is to symbolise the equality of power and responsibility in the marriage.

step1.meaning:
With the promise to nourish each other,
I take this first step with you.

step2.meaning:
With the determination to grow together in physical, mental and spiritual strength,
I take this second step with you.

step3.meaning:
With the promise to preserve our wealth and prosperity,
I take this third step with you.

step4.meaning:
With the vow to live together in happiness and harmony,
I take this fourth step with you.

step5.meaning:
With the promise to care for our healthy and long-lived children,
I take this fifth step with you.

step6.meaning:
With the vow to remain together through all the seasons and responsibilities of life,
I take this sixth step with you.

step7.meaning:
With the promise of everlasting and true companionship,
I take this seventh step with you.

lajaHoma.title: Lājā Homa
lajaHoma.subtitle: The offering of grain
lajaHoma.body: This shall comprise the bride’s own offering to the sacrificial fire. As she is forbidden to do it herself, her brother helps her. He gives her a handful of parched rice grains, which she hands to the bridegroom, who, on her behalf, feeds it into the fire. Through this food offering, the bride seeks a long life for her husband and propagation of the family. Participation of the bride’s family members indicates the continuance of links between the two families, even after marriage. The couple circles around the fire three times, and the feeding of the fire with parched rice, is repeated thrice.

ashmarohana.title: Aśmārohaṇa
ashmarohana.subtitle: The stepping on a stone
ashmarohana.body: Holding the bride’s left foot toe, the bridegroom helps her tread on a grindstone kept on the right side of the fire. The Manthras says: "Mount up this stone. Let thy mind be rock-firm, unperturbed by the trials and tribulations of life?

custom1790514236467.title: Ganapathi Puja ( Vigneshwara Pujai)
custom1790514236467.subtitle: Prelude to the Marriage, a prayer to the God of Beginnings and wisdom
custom1790514236467.body: As in an inauguration of any function, so also in a marriage – Ganapati, the God of Initiation, is invoked to keep away all impediments.

custom1790514385010.title: Navagraha Puja
custom1790514385010.subtitle: Prayer  to the 9 Astral Planets
custom1790514385010.body: This is performed to propitiate the nine astral planets that are believed to rule over man’s destiny.

custom1790514697611.title: Vratham
custom1790514697611.subtitle: The Sacred Observance
custom1790514697611.body: The marriage ceremonies begin with the Vratham performed separately by the bride and the groom. For the bride, it means the tying of the KAPPU – the holy thread on her wrist, which is meant to ward off all evil spirits. It symbolises a kind of protective armour for the bride. For the groom, the various Gods – Indra, Soma, Chandra, Agni. From there on, the groom prepares himself for a new chapter in his life as a householder or Grihasta. The days of his bachelorhood or brahmacharya are now over and the acceptance of this is all that the Vratham is about.

custom1790514817642.title: Pālikai  (Palikai Talitthul)
custom1790514817642.subtitle: SEEDS SOWING
custom1790514817642.body: This is a fertility rite. Paalikais are five earthen pots prepared a day earlier – pots spread at the base with mango leaves (mavilai) and sand; nine kinds of pre-soaked cereals are ceremonially sown in these pots by five Sumangalis(Married ladies). After the marriage, the sprouted seedlings are released in a river or pool by kanyas(Unmarried girls). This ritual invokes the blessings of the eight-direction-quartered guardian angels for a healthy life and progeny for the couple.

custom1790514930333.title: Nāndī Śrāddham
custom1790514930333.subtitle: Honouring the ancestors and seeking their blessings
custom1790514930333.body: There are several presiding deities – the Nandi Devatas. To propitiate them, a leaf-laden branch of the pipal tree is installed, and an ablution with milk is performed by five Sumangalis (housewives with husbands living). This puja is followed by a presentation of a dhoti and a saree to the marrying couple.

custom1790515143408.title: Kāśī Yātrā
custom1790515143408.subtitle: The Renunciation of Ascetic Life
custom1790515143408.body: This is a very important part of the ceremony. Immediately after his student life, the young bachelor has two alternatives before him – Married life ( Grihasta ) or asceticism (Sanyas). Being by nature escapist, he prefers the ascetic life to the tribulations of married life. He therefore ‘makes his way’ to Kasi (VARANASI), complete with slippers, umbrella, bamboo fan, etc. On his way, the bride’s father intervenes and advises him of the superiority of married life to ascetic life. He also promises to give him his daughter as a companion to face the challenge of life. The umbrella is to remain with the groom, to remind him in the future of this advice.

custom1790515353939.title: Mālāparivartanam (Malai Mattal)
custom1790515353939.subtitle: Exchange of garlands
custom1790515353939.body: The bride and the groom are lifted onto the shoulders of their respective uncles, and in that position they garland each other thrice for a complete union. A garland worn by a person should not be used by another, ordain our shastras. Here the exchange of garlands symbolises their unification – as one soul in two bodies. It is inward acceptance by each of the very fragrance of the other

custom1790515506877.title: Oonjhal
custom1790515506877.subtitle: The Swing Ceremony
custom1790515506877.body: Then, the marrying couple is seated on a swing ( OONCHAL); they rock forth and back, as the ladies around sing – LAALI, songs to praise to the couple. The chains of the swing signify the eternal Karmic link with Almighty above; the to-and-fro motion represent the undulating sea-waves of life; yet, in mind and body they shall move in harmony unperturbed, steady and stable.

custom1790515807333.title: Madhuparkam
custom1790515807333.subtitle: The Confirmation
custom1790515807333.body:
Madhuparkam is a part of the aforesaid ritual. It has the bride’s father offering a mixture of curd, gee and honey to the groom.Curd, ghee and honey, all are considered to be good for one's health. Besides, these edibles are believed to be auspicious and impart good effects to whatsoever associated with it.
On the girl’s head, a ring made with Kusa, the sacred grass called DARBHA, is placed, and over it, is placed a yoke; the Gold Mangal Sutra ( or THAALI ) is placed right on the aperture of the yoke, and water is poured through the aperture. The Mantras chanted at this time, say:
"Let this gold multiply your wealth? Let this water purify your married life, and may your prosperity increase. Offer yourself to your husband? "
The bride then is given an auspicious ablution, and an exclusive new KOORAI Saree is draped around her – this is done by the sister of the bridegroom.
To bride in her new saree, a belt made of reed-grass is tied around the waist. The manthras chant:
"She standeth here, pure before the holy fire, as one blessed with boons of a good mind, a healthy body, life-long companionship of her husband ( Sumangali Bhagyam ) and children with long life. She standeth as one who is avowed to stand by her husband virtuously. Be she tied with this red-grass rope, to the sacrament of marriage? "
Thanks giving vedic hymns follow to the celestial caretakers of her childhood: the Deities of SOMA, GANDHARVA and AGNI. Having attained nobility, the girl is now free to be given over to the care of the human – her man.
The Vedic concepts underlying this ritual is figuratively this: that in her infant stage, SOMA had given her coolness of the moon, and strength; in the next stage, GANDHARVA had given her bodily beauty; and lastly AGNI gave her passions.
The father of the bride, while offering his daughter chants: "I offer you my daughter, a maiden virtuous, good-natured, very wise, decked with ornaments to the best of my ability-; that she shall guard the Dharma, Wealth, and Love?

custom1790515894191.title: Māṅgalya Dhāraṇam
custom1790515894191.subtitle: Groom ties the Wedding Necklace
custom1790515894191.body: Next, timed to exact auspicious hour, is the tying of the Mangala Sutra ( Thaali ). The bride seated over a sheaf of grain-laden hay, looking eastward, and the bridegroom facing westward, ties the gold Mangala Sutra around the neck of the bride. As he does so, the Nadaswaram drums are beaten loud and fast, so as to muffle any inauspicious sounds at the critical hour. This is called Getti Melam; as it sounds, the Sumangali ladies sing "GOURIKALYANAME,VAIBHOGAMAY" Three knots are tied – the first one by the bridegroom, the other two knots by his sister to make the bride a parts of the boy’s family. The Vedic hymn recited by the bridegroom when he ties the knot, is: " Praying the Almighty that I be blessed with a long life, I tie this knot around your neck, oh soubhaygavati, may providence bestow on you a fulfilling life of a ‘Sumangalis’ for a hundred years to come? "

custom1790516070533.title: Pradhāna Homam
custom1790516070533.subtitle: Making the Fire the witness
custom1790516070533.body: A crucial part of the wedding is the homage paid by the couple to AGNI, the fire god. They circle around the fire and feed it with ghee and twigs of nine types of trees as sacrificial fuel. The fumes that arise are supposed to possess medicinal, curative, and cleansing effects on the bodies of the couple. AGNI, the mightiest power in the cosmos, the sacred purifier, the all-round benefactor, is deemed a witness to the marriage (AGNI SAAKSHI )

custom1790516234957.title: Akshidai (Ashirwadam)
custom1790516234957.subtitle: Showering of blessings
custom1790516234957.body: Akshadai, i.e. rice-grains coated with turmeric , are showered on the couple, by PRIEST(Vadhyar),elders and invitees – as benediction.

custom1790516288395.title: Griha Pravesham
custom1790516288395.subtitle: Entering the Husband's home
custom1790516288395.body: Taking with her fire from the Laaja Homam, the bride takes leave of her home and enters the new home of her in-laws. The Vedic hymns now sound like the mother’s words of advice to her daughter: "Be the queen of your husband’s home. May your husband glorify your virtues; conduct yourself in such a way that you win your mother-in-law’s love, and be in the good books of your sister-in-law."

custom1790516354628.title: Nalungu
custom1790516354628.subtitle: The Playful Blessing
custom1790516354628.body:
The evening of the marriage day is the time to relax and play. The newly wed wife calls her husband for play, inviting him through a song. Much to the merriment of one and all gathered, there follows list of playful items: the bride anointing the groom’s feet with colour paste ; fanning him, showing him a mirror; breaking papads over each other’s head; wrenching the betel pack from each other’s hand; rolling the coconut from one to another as in ball-play; and so on. During these items, the ladies sing songs poking fun at the bride, groom and the in-laws.
These events brings out many qualities of the bride and the groom – sporting spirit, kindness, strength, co-operative nature etc

custom1790516553191.title: Rātri Homa
custom1790516553191.subtitle: The night time Homas
custom1790516553191.body:
• THE JAYAATHI HOMAM – is performed to propitiate the Gandharvas and deities.
• PRAVESA HOMAM – is done to solemnise the bride’s entry in to the husband’s home. The sacrificial fire is brought along by the bride.
• SESHA HOMAM – is Fire oblation with the residual ghee, a little of which is sprinkled on the bride’s head four times.

custom1790516652284.title: Arundathi Darshanam
custom1790516652284.subtitle: Showing her the Arundathi Star (Alcor of Ursa Major)
custom1790516652284.body: Next, he shows her the Star ARUNDHATI ( of the SAPTHA RISHI Constellation ), as well as DHRUVA, the pole star. Arundhati, the wife of VASISHTA Maharishi, is exemplified as an ideal wife, the embodiment of chastity. DHRUVA is the one who attained immortality through single-minded devotion and perseverance – virtues to be emulated throughout married life

custom1790516846397.title: Tāmbūla Carvaṇam & Phala Dānam
custom1790516846397.subtitle: Beetle leaves and fruits
custom1790516846397.body: The girl’s brother gives the ceremonial first betel to the couple to chew. Certain other gifts are made to bless the couple with children and long life.

custom1790516912049.title: Mangala Arathi
custom1790516912049.subtitle: The Auspicious Offering of Light.
custom1790516912049.body: A solution of lime and turmeric powder, and in colour, is prepared on a plate, circled around, and thrown away to ward off the evil eye. This is done a number of times during the entire wedding ceremony and at the end.
